key_insight: Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP) separates robot intelligence into understanding what to do and learning how to move. It builds on pretrained vision-language knowledge, then uses simulated tasks to teach robot control through a simple tool interface.
problem_solved: Bridging the gap between interpreting task instructions in a visual scene and executing the robot movements needed to complete them, with compositional generalization as the central goal.
method: Use a pretrained 27B-parameter vision-language model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning.
Connect the model to robot controls through a simple tool harness.
Apply supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on simple simulated tasks to teach movement.
impact: ZAP offers practitioners a recipe for combining pretrained semantic knowledge with simulation-based control learning. The abstract does not report quantitative results, so its generalization performance and real-world reliability remain unquantified here.
visual_elements: Two-part diagram: pretraining supplies 'what'; simulation teaches 'how'.
Training pipeline: pretrained model → supervised fine-tuning → GRPO → robot policy.
Control-loop illustration: scene and instruction → model → tool harness → robot action.
Compositional-task grid showing familiar objects, instructions, and actions recombined into new tasks.
paper_title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
paper_authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew
